newsitem.title: CANADA: Inco strike trims nickel firm's Q2 earnings.
newsitem.headline: Inco strike trims nickel firm's Q2 earnings.

text.p: Canada's Inco Ltd. , the Western world's largest nickel producer, reported sharply weaker second-quarter earnings on Monday due to a long strike at its Sudbury, Ontario, operations.
Toronto-based Inco said net income for the second quarter fell to $16 million, or 5 cents a share, from $61 million, or 47 cents a share, a year ago.
Sales were $645 million, down from $667 million a year earlier.
A 26-day strike at Inco's Ontario division, which ended June 28, resulted in an after-tax cost of $20 million, or 12 cents a share, in the second quarter.
Inco also tied the drop in second-quarter earnings to lower prices for nickel, cobalt and copper, and costs associated with the rebuild of furnace No. 1 at P.T. Inco in Indonesia.
The second-quarter earnings were far below analysts' consensus estimates of about 15 cents a share. Some analysts said they had expected Inco to account for the strike in the third quarter.

Inco stock shrugged off the results and surged on stronger nickel prices, analysts said. The stock jumped C$1.30 to C$42.55 on active trading of 1.2 million shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange. In New York, Inco rose $1.19 to $30.625.
"When you look at what nickel prices have done these last few days, that obviously makes a difference," said Craig Temby, an analyst at J.B. Were and Son Inc.
The London Metal Exchange three-month nickel price has gained $610 to $7,385 a metric ton in the past two trading days.
Meanwhile, an aboriginal group said on Monday it may blockade ships ferrying materials to Inco's huge Voisey's Bay project in Labrador for construction of an airstrip and road this summer.

The Innu Nation and Labrador Inuit Association earlier this month lost a court battle to halt the construction projects, which they argued should fall under a broader environmental review of the project.
The groups are appealing the court ruling, but Innu Nation President Katie Rich said they may take stronger action.

"We are thinking of blocking the ships that will be going to Voisey's Bay. We think the airstrip and the road are part of the whole project and should also go through environmental assessment," Rich said in a telephone interview.
